name: btfs
why: A filesystem backed by BitTorrent swarms, mounting torrent contents as if they were local files, a genuinely odd transform of a familiar protocol.

brief.what_it_is: BTFS is a FUSE filesystem that mounts a .torrent file or magnet link as a read-only directory. You give it a torrent and an empty mount point, and the torrent's contents appear as ordinary files that tools like ls, cat, and cp can read. The README says file contents are downloaded from the swarm on demand as applications read them, and that media players such as vlc and mplayer work without changes.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to use any torrent as a directory in your file tree, so that existing applications can consume torrent contents without a separate BitTorrent client workflow. It gives no further motivation.
brief.how_it_works: The README says contents are downloaded on demand as applications read them, so reads drive which pieces are fetched. It does not describe the internals further. The Linux dependency list names libtorrent and libcurl, which suggests libtorrent handles the swarm work, but the README does not say so.

commands_seen.cmd: $ brew install --cask macfuse libtorrent-rasterbar autoconf automake pkg-config
commands_seen.context: Installs the macOS build dependencies: macFUSE, libtorrent, and the autotools.

brief.install_notes: Packages exist for Debian/Ubuntu (apt-get install btfs), Arch (pacman -S btfs), Gentoo (emerge -av btfs), Fedora (dnf install fuse-btfs), Fedora OSTree (rpm-ostree install fuse-btfs), and openSUSE (zypper install btfs). On Linux the README lists fuse3, libtorrent (libtorrent-rasterbar8 on Ubuntu 22.04), and libcurl as dependencies. Building from git on Debian or Ubuntu needs autoconf, automake, libfuse3-dev, libtorrent-rasterbar-dev, libcurl4-openssl-dev, and g++, followed by autoreconf -i, ./configure, and make. On macOS, brew install is the route, and building from source needs the macfuse cask plus libtorrent-rasterbar. No accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration appear in the README.
brief.standout: It turns a torrent swarm into an ordinary read-only directory that unmodified programs can open, with pieces fetched as reads happen, so a player can start a video before the download is complete. Most torrent tools expect you to manage a download, not browse one as a filesystem.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no release version, date, changelog, or last-commit information, and the fetch tool returned only the README, so I could not check recency. The README does list packages in several distributions, which suggests it has been around for a while, but that is an inference.
brief.caveats: The mount is read-only, as the README states. Linux needs FUSE 3 and libtorrent and libcurl. Building from source needs several autotools and development packages, and macOS needs the macFUSE cask. The README does not mention licensing, platform support beyond Linux and macOS, or known limitations. The homepage fetch succeeded, so this is not a reachability problem.
quotes: With BTFS, you can mount any **.torrent** file or **magnet link** and then use it as any read-only directory in your file tree.
The contents of the files will be downloaded on-demand as they are read by applications.
Tools like **ls**, **cat** and **cp** works as expected. Applications like **vlc** and **mplayer** can also work without changes.

judge.reason: Mounting a torrent as a read-only directory lets ordinary programs browse or play files while swarm pieces download on demand—a genuinely surprising protocol-to-filesystem transform.

entry.title: btfs
entry.tldr: Mounts a .torrent file or magnet link as a read-only directory, so ls, cat and video players can read files that download from the swarm as they are opened.
entry.deeper_look:
btfs is a FUSE filesystem. You give it a .torrent file or a magnet link and an empty directory, and the torrent's contents show up as ordinary files there. The README says the data is downloaded on demand as applications read it, so nothing needs to be fetched in full before you start looking around.

The idea underneath is that a filesystem is a very old, very general interface, and almost every program already speaks it. Put a network protocol behind that interface and unmodified tools can use it with no knowledge of the protocol. The README says ls, cat and cp work as expected, and that players such as vlc and mplayer work without changes. Because reads drive what gets fetched, a player can begin a video before the whole file has arrived.

The README does not describe the internals. The dependency list names libtorrent-rasterbar and curl, which suggests libtorrent handles the swarm side, but that is an inference. The mount is read-only. Installing the formula also gives you `btfsstat` and `btplay`, which the brief does not document.

It is a small tool with a clear premise, and a good way to see what happens when a download stops being a task and becomes a place.
entry.install:
brew install btfs
# macOS also needs macFUSE: brew install --cask macfuse
# Debian/Ubuntu: apt-get install btfs
# Needs a FUSE implementation (FUSE 3 on Linux) and an empty directory to mount onto.

try_this.what_happens: Mounts the torrent onto the existing empty directory mnt, and its files appear there as read-only entries.
Run from inside mnt, this plays a file straight from the mounted torrent, fetching pieces as vlc reads them.
Unmounts the directory and shuts down the btfs mount.

entry.whats_unique: It turns a torrent swarm into a plain directory that unmodified programs can open, rather than a download you manage in a client.
entry.caveats: The README gives no version or date, so how actively it is maintained is unclear, and the mount is read-only and needs FUSE (macFUSE on macOS).
